Clinical Vignette: Patient A.

Patient A. is a sixty-year-old midwife who has worked in the same community hospital for over thirty years. She lives with her partner of twenty years, a retired carpenter. She came to therapy at the urging of her partner, who has grown increasingly worried about her withdrawal and the episodes of what she calls "the shaking spells."

The event that changed everything happened two years ago, during a routine delivery. The patient was assisting a laboring woman when a maintenance crew entered the room unannounced to strip old floor wax. The chemical smell – a sweet, acrid odor she later learned contained a high concentration of toluene – spread quickly. The patient tried to wave them out, but they insisted the work had already begun. She spent the next forty minutes in that room, breathing the fumes while attending to the mother and newborn. She remembers a headache blooming behind her eyes, a metallic taste in her mouth, and the vague sense that something was wrong. She completed the shift but woke the next morning with a splitting migraine, nausea, and a feeling of being "chemically poisoned."

Since that day, she has avoided the labor and delivery floor where the spill occurred. She took a leave of absence initially, then returned only to the prenatal clinic – a quieter, cleaner space. She cannot walk past the hospital maintenance corridors; the faintest whiff of cleaning solution sends her into a spiral of dizziness and panic. She has asked her partner to remove all scented products from their home: no candles, no laundry detergent with fragrance, no air freshener. Even the smell of a neighbor's barbecue drifts in through a window, she says, and she feels her throat close.

The traumatic memory intrudes without warning. During a prenatal visit last month, the patient was monitoring a fetal heartbeat when the sound of a floor buffer down the hall triggered a flashback so vivid she could taste the wax again. She excused herself, locked herself in a staff bathroom, and dry-heaved for ten minutes. She now wears an N95 mask even in the clinic, which her colleagues find odd. She has stopped eating lunch in the break room because someone reheated a meal in a plastic container that seemed to give off a chemical odor.

Her sleep is broken. She wakes at three or four in the morning, certain she can smell the toxin on her own skin, and she will shower for nearly an hour, scrubbing until her shoulders are raw. Her partner has learned not to touch her after a shower; she flinches. She describes feeling "permanently contaminated." She has started checking the labels of every household product, and she once drove forty minutes to a natural market to buy vinegar for cleaning because bleach triggers her.

The patient's mood has darkened. She used to be animated, laughing easily with expectant mothers. Now she avoids eye contact. She tells me she feels "hollowed out." She cannot drive past the hospital without her heart racing. She no longer attends family gatherings because someone might be wearing perfume. Her partner has become her buffer, doing the grocery shopping and answering the phone.

She has not told her colleagues the full story. She fears being seen as weak or overly sensitive. When a younger midwife asked why she changed floors, the patient said only, "I needed a change." She carries guilt about leaving the women she used to serve – "those mothers trusted me," she said, her voice flat. She also worries that the chemical exposure may have permanently damaged her own body. She has seen multiple doctors, none of whom could find a physiological cause for her ongoing symptoms. Each negative test only deepens her sense of isolation.

She spends her days off in the garden, wearing gloves and a mask if the neighbor's fertilizer is blowing. She rarely leaves the house otherwise. Her partner tells me she cries silently at night, but when he asks, she says, "I just can't stop remembering that room."

The patient's score on the PCL-5 is 54, consistent with severe posttraumatic stress. She has never before sought therapy and remains uncertain whether talking can help "a chemical stuck inside me."
